title: Milia
summary: Milia are tiny (1–2 mm) white keratin cysts just under the epidermis. Primary milia are common in newborns and on the face; secondary milia follow blistering, trauma, dermabrasion or potent topical steroids. Harmless; usually left alone.

what: **Milia** are 1–2 mm superficial **keratin cysts** (tiny epidermoid cysts). **Primary** milia arise spontaneously (up to half of newborns; also adults on the eyelids and cheeks). **Secondary** milia follow blistering, trauma, burns, dermabrasion or potent topical steroids.
cause: Primary milia form from the lower **infundibulum of vellus hairs**; secondary milia form when damaged sweat ducts, follicles or epidermis become trapped during healing.

list: Firm, pearly **white or yellow** dome papules, 1–2 mm.
Face (eyelids, cheeks, nose) in primary milia; at sites of previous blisters or scars in secondary milia (e.g. hands in porphyria cutanea tarda or epidermolysis bullosa).
Neonatal milia: nose and cheeks; resolve within weeks.

diagnosis: Clinical. Dermoscopy shows a white-yellow globule. Look for a cause of secondary milia (blistering disease, PCT, steroid use).

list: **Comedones** (acne): central keratin plug in a follicle, other acne lesions.
**Syringoma**: skin-coloured papules on the lower eyelids.
**Sebaceous hyperplasia**: yellow umbilicated papules with crown vessels.
**Molluscum contagiosum**: umbilicated, pearly papules, often in children.
If cosmetically troublesome: de-roofing with a sterile needle and gentle expression (de-roofing and extraction).
Topical retinoids may help multiple milia; avoid potent steroids that provoke them.
Milia on scarred, fragile skin of the backs of the hands: think **porphyria cutanea tarda** or epidermolysis bullosa acquisita.
Milia are **cysts**, not blocked sebaceous glands; squeezing without de-roofing does not work.
